(1) _tell_crm ignores `stored`: 4 red. (2) save() returns True on fallback even with Redis configured: 6 red. (3) release() uses time.time() instead of `at`, the spec's 'end ignores the passed at' mutation moved to its new home: 2 red. (4) hand_back ignores `reached`: 1 red. (5) _take_over ignores hold()'s answer: 2 red, both new tests in test_crm_send.py. So every new branch has a test that bites. Those tests use a fake store whose set() raises ConnectionError, the same kind of failure user_store's real redis client raises. They are not stubs of the code under test. That is synthetic, but it stands in for exactly the thing round 3's P3-1 described: another thread's _go_offline.

self_check.spec_deviation: The spec said handover.end(profile, at=None). The commit instead adds handover.release(profile, at) and hold(profile, reason), and end() goes back to taking no `at`. The spec's promise that existing callers do not change still holds (console.py:635 and whatsapp_webhook.py:768 call end(profile) unchanged). The spec's mutation check still applies, under release (mutation 3 above). I accept this as justified. The split lets the CRM-facing callers get a per-write 'reached Redis' answer without changing begin/end/touch's return contract, which tools/human.py depends on (it must still go silent on a memory-only takeover). Not raised: a hand-back over two held records where the first release reaches Redis and the second falls back. It answers 503 after an active=false event has already been queued for the first record. This needs Redis to fail in the microseconds between two saves, and it is the same as at 38556e7, not something this commit introduced.

phase2.rebuttals: I read the round-3 entry in todo.md (the diff 38556e7..d161916). Most of it holds, and I checked it. (1) 'Existing callers do not read save()'s return': holds. I grepped every user_store.save call under backend/app and only handover.py uses the return value. (2) 'begin/touch/end keep their semantics and signatures for existing callers': holds. begin still returns True on a memory-only takeover. That matters because tools/human.py:67 must still go silent, and console.py and whatsapp_webhook.py call end(profile) unchanged. (3) 'A null handover in the answer is the contract's own word for this step failing': holds, and with it the answer and the event now agree (both silent). Round 3's repro is green. (4) The mutation counts match mine once you allow for their counting round 3's repro inside the run. Theirs: save-always-True 7, send-ignores-hold 3, hand_back-ignores-release 1. Mine, suite only and net of seed_console: 6, 2, 1. (5) The one argument that is only partly true: 'the read side has no per-call answer to ask, so the offline() check after the reads stays'. That is a choice, not a fact: get() could report where its answer came from, the way save() now does. It is acceptable as a choice, though. As written, offline() after the read can go wrong only two ways. One is a spurious 503 when another thread trips the breaker after a good read; that is the safe direction, and a retry fixes it. The other is the microsecond false not_active at the window boundary that round 2 already recorded. Neither is new, so I do not raise it. One process point I did not check myself: their mutation 'change _tell_crm back to asking offline()' -> 1 failed. My mutation removed the check entirely instead, so the race test's power against exactly that regression is their claim, not my result.
phase2.blind_spot: Their admissions this round are: the same shape of mistake for the third time (a rule stated in the commit message and applied to one channel only); a global flag used as a stand-in for one call's result; a mutation that silently did not apply because of CRLF and would have read as 'caught'; and 'nobody re-reviews this fix'. None of them is a code defect I missed. The last one is exactly what this round is, and the CRLF one is about their tooling. I did nearly miss a version of it, though: my first mutation script had a placeholder entry I skipped by hand, and I only trusted the others because each replacement was checked for NO MATCH before running. Without that guard, an unapplied mutation would have shown up as the baseline '2 failed' and I could have misread a count. The real blind spot of this round is end to end: like rounds 1-3, nothing here was exercised against the real acuven_crm_demo consumer. The whole argument rests on the CRM storing the synchronous answer first and treating handover:null and a non-200 hand-back the way the contract says. That gets checked only at the phone acceptance test after push, not by any round of this review.
